title: CBSE Class 12 Economics · Practice paper 2
subject: Economics
label: Practice paper
instr: This question paper contains 34 questions. All questions are compulsory.

This question paper contains two sections:
Section A: Macroeconomics (40 marks), questions 1 to 17
Section B: Indian Economic Development (40 marks), questions 18 to 34
This paper contains 20 multiple choice type questions of 1 mark each.
This paper contains 4 short answer type questions of 3 marks each, to be answered in 60 to 80 words.
This paper contains 6 short answer type questions of 4 marks each, to be answered in 80 to 100 words.
This paper contains 4 long answer type questions of 6 marks each, to be answered in 100 to 150 words.
Attempt all parts of a question together.
Internal choices of the board paper are not included: each question has one version.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Identify which of the following are stock variables.
(i) Depreciation of machines during 2025-26
(ii) Capital stock of a firm on 1 April 2025
(iii) Change in stock (inventory) during 2025-26
(iv) Bank deposits held by a household on 31 March 2026
(Choose the correct option)
questions.sol: A stock is measured at a point of time, while a flow is measured over a period of time. Capital stock on a date and bank deposits on a date are stocks. Depreciation during a year and change in stock during a year are flows.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following statements carefully:
Statement 1: Under a barter system, a double coincidence of wants is not needed for an exchange to take place.
Statement 2: Money serves as a standard of deferred payments, as future payments such as loan repayments can be stated in terms of money.
In light of the given statements, choose the correct option from the following:
options: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.
questions.sol: Statement 1 is false: barter needs a double coincidence of wants, as each party must want what the other offers. Statement 2 is true: debts payable in the future are stated in money, so money acts as a standard of deferred payments.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Ceteris paribus, a large inflow of foreign investment into India sets off a chain of effects in the foreign exchange market.
Identify which of the following sequences explains this process.
(i) Supply of US dollars in the foreign exchange market rises
(ii) Indian exports become costlier for foreign buyers
(iii) Rupee price of the US dollar falls
(Choose the correct option)
questions.sol: Foreign investors bring in dollars, so the supply of dollars rises; with demand unchanged, the rupee price of the dollar falls (the rupee appreciates); foreign buyers then need more dollars to buy the same rupee value of goods, so Indian exports become costlier for them.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
For a hypothetical economy: Gross Domestic Product at market price = ₹5,000 crore, consumption of fixed capital = ₹400 crore, net factor income from abroad = ($-$) ₹100 crore and net indirect taxes = ₹300 crore.
The value of National Income (Net National Product at factor cost) is ₹ ________ crore.
(Choose the correct option to fill up the blank)
questions.sol: NNP at FC = GDP at MP $-$ Consumption of fixed capital + NFIA $-$ Net indirect taxes = 5,000 $-$ 400 + ($-$100) $-$ 300 = ₹4,200 crore.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Which of the following is always true?
(Choose the correct option)
options: APC can never be greater than 1
questions.sol: Every addition to income is either consumed or saved, so $\Delta C + \Delta S = \Delta Y$, which gives MPC + MPS = 1. Below the break-even level of income, consumption exceeds income, so APC is greater than 1 and APS is negative.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
In an economy, currency held by the public is ₹1,20,000 crore, net demand deposits held by commercial banks are ₹80,000 crore and net time deposits with commercial banks are ₹1,50,000 crore.
The money supply (M1) of the economy is ₹ ________ crore.
(Choose the correct option to fill up the blank)
questions.sol: M1 = Currency held by the public + Net demand deposits held by commercial banks = 1,20,000 + 80,000 = ₹2,00,000 crore. Time deposits are not part of M1.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following statements: Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Choose the correct option from those given below:
Assertion (A): A rise in the price of foreign currency makes imports cheaper for the residents of a country.
Reason (R): The demand for foreign exchange falls when its price rises.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.sol: A is false: when foreign currency becomes costlier, residents must pay more domestic currency for the same imports, so imports become costlier. R is true: as foreign exchange becomes costlier, imports become costlier and fewer are bought, so the demand for foreign exchange falls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Which of the following will be included in the estimation of India's Gross Domestic Product?
(i) Purchase of a second-hand car from a neighbour
(ii) Commission paid to a dealer for arranging the sale of a second-hand car
(iii) Old-age pension paid by the government
(iv) Scholarship given by the government to a student
(Choose the correct option)
questions.sol: The commission is payment for a productive service rendered in the current year, so it is included. The second-hand car was already counted when it was produced, and pensions and scholarships are transfer payments with no production in return.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
"The central bank keeps the accounts of the central and state governments, receives and makes payments on their behalf and manages their borrowings."
Identify the function of the central bank described above.
(Choose the correct option)
questions.sol: Keeping government accounts, making and receiving payments for the government and managing public debt are part of the central bank's role as banker, agent and adviser to the government.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
In an economy, the marginal propensity to consume is 0.9. To raise income by ₹5,000 crore, investment must increase by ₹ ________ crore.
(Choose the correct option to fill up the blank)
questions.sol: Multiplier $k = \frac{1}{1 - MPC} = \frac{1}{0.1} = 10$. Required increase in investment $= \frac{\Delta Y}{k} = \frac{5{,}000}{10}$ = ₹500 crore.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Giving a valid reason, state whether the following will be included in the national income of India:
(a) Profit earned by a branch of an Indian bank located in Singapore
(b) Old-age pension paid by the government to retired citizens
(c) Purchase of newly issued shares of an Indian company by a household
questions.model:
(a) Included. National income (NNP at factor cost) includes net factor income from abroad. The profit is a factor income earned abroad by a normal resident of India (the Indian bank).
(b) Not included. Old-age pension is a transfer payment; no productive service is rendered in return for it in the current year.
(c) Not included. Purchase of shares is only a financial transaction (a transfer of ownership claims); it does not add to the flow of goods and services.

points.t: (a) Included
Reason: factor income earned abroad by a resident, part of NFIA
(b) Not included
Reason: transfer payment, no productive service in return
(c) Not included
Reason: financial transaction, no production of goods or services

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Assume that the entire banking system works as a single bank, all transactions are routed through banks and the legal reserve ratio is 25%. Explain the process of money creation by commercial banks when a fresh deposit of ₹1,000 is made.
questions.model:
When ₹1,000 is deposited, the bank keeps 25% of it, that is ₹250, as reserves and lends the remaining ₹750.
The borrowers spend the ₹750, and since all transactions are routed through banks, it comes back to the banking system as fresh deposits. The bank again keeps 25% (₹187.50) as reserves and lends ₹562.50. This chain of lending and re-depositing goes on, each round smaller than the last, until the total reserves equal the initial deposit of ₹1,000.
Total deposits created = Initial deposit $\times \frac{1}{LRR} = 1{,}000 \times \frac{1}{0.25}$ = ₹4,000. So an initial deposit of ₹1,000 leads to total deposits of ₹4,000.

points.t: Bank keeps 25% (₹250) as reserves and lends the remaining ₹750
Loans come back as fresh deposits and the lending process repeats in smaller rounds
Total deposits = 1,000 $\times$ 1/0.25 = ₹4,000

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
From the following data relating to a firm, calculate its Net Value Added at factor cost.
S. No.ItemsAmount (in ₹ crore)
(i)Domestic sales1,300
(ii)Exports200
(iii)Change in stock(-) 100
(iv)Purchase of raw materials600
(v)Depreciation80
(vi)Net indirect taxes70
questions.model:
Value of output = Domestic sales + Exports + Change in stock = 1,300 + 200 + ($-$100) = ₹1,400 crore
Gross Value Added at market price = Value of output $-$ Intermediate consumption = 1,400 $-$ 600 = ₹800 crore
Net Value Added at factor cost = GVA at MP $-$ Depreciation $-$ Net indirect taxes = 800 $-$ 80 $-$ 70
= ₹650 crore

points.t: Value of output = 1,300 + 200 + ($-$100) = ₹1,400 crore
GVA at MP = 1,400 $-$ 600 = ₹800 crore
Correct formula: NVA at FC = GVA at MP $-$ Depreciation $-$ Net indirect taxes
Correct answer: ₹650 crore

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following text carefully:
The exchange rate of a country's currency is normally determined by the demand for and supply of foreign exchange in the market. Last month, however, the currency fell sharply against the US dollar within a few days. The country's central bank then sold US dollars from its foreign exchange reserves to limit the fall.

parts.q: (I) Identify the exchange rate system indicated in the text and explain it.
parts.model: The system is the managed floating exchange rate system. Under it, the exchange rate is mainly determined by market forces of demand and supply, but the central bank intervenes by buying or selling foreign currency to limit large fluctuations in the exchange rate.

points.t: Managed floating exchange rate system
Rate set by market forces, with central bank intervention to limit fluctuations

parts.q: (II) Explain how the sale of US dollars by the central bank helps to limit the fall of the domestic currency.
parts.model: When the central bank sells dollars from its reserves, the supply of dollars in the foreign exchange market increases. With demand unchanged, the price of the dollar in terms of domestic currency falls (or rises less than it otherwise would). So the domestic currency regains value or stops falling, and the exchange rate is stabilised.

points.t: Sale of dollars increases the supply of dollars in the foreign exchange market
Price of the dollar falls/rises less, so the fall of the domestic currency is checked

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In a hypothetical economy, the equilibrium level of income is ₹5,000 crore, while the full employment level of income is ₹6,000 crore.

parts.q: (I) Identify the problem faced by the economy and state its effect on output and employment.
parts.model:
The economy faces deficient demand: aggregate demand is less than aggregate supply at the full employment level, so equilibrium is reached below full employment.
Output (₹5,000 crore) is below the full employment level, so there is involuntary unemployment: some people willing to work at the existing wage do not get work.

points.t: Deficient demand (AD less than AS at full employment)
Output below full employment level, causing involuntary unemployment

parts.q: (II) Explain how a reduction in the cash reserve ratio by the central bank can help to correct this problem.
parts.model: Cash reserve ratio is the minimum percentage of deposits that commercial banks must keep as cash reserves with the central bank. When it is reduced, banks have more funds available to lend, and their capacity to create credit rises. More credit is available at lower cost, so investment and consumption spending rise. Aggregate demand increases, which raises output and employment towards the full employment level.

points.t: Lower CRR frees funds with banks and raises their credit creation capacity
More credit raises investment/consumption, so AD, output and employment rise

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following text carefully and answer the questions that follow.
The Finance Minister of the hypothetical country of Sundaram presented the budget for 2026-27 with the following estimates (in ₹ crore):
ItemAmount
Tax revenue16,000
Non-tax revenue4,000
Recovery of loans600
Disinvestment proceeds400
Borrowings14,000
Revenue expenditure26,000
of which: interest payments7,000
Capital expenditure9,000
Opposition members criticised the budget. They said that a large part of the government's borrowing was being used to pay interest on past loans and to meet day-to-day expenses rather than to build assets.

parts.q: (I) Classify disinvestment proceeds as a revenue receipt or a capital receipt, giving a reason.
parts.model: Capital receipt, because disinvestment (sale of the government's shares in public sector enterprises) reduces the assets of the government.

points.t: Capital receipt
Reason: it reduces the assets of the government

parts.q: (II) Calculate the revenue deficit and the fiscal deficit of Sundaram.
parts.model:
Revenue receipts = 16,000 + 4,000 = ₹20,000 crore
Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure $-$ Revenue receipts = 26,000 $-$ 20,000 = ₹6,000 crore
Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure $-$ (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts)
= (26,000 + 9,000) $-$ (20,000 + 600 + 400) = 35,000 $-$ 21,000 = ₹14,000 crore
(This equals the borrowings of ₹14,000 crore.)

points.t: Revenue deficit = 26,000 $-$ 20,000 = ₹6,000 crore
Fiscal deficit = 35,000 $-$ 21,000 = ₹14,000 crore

parts.q: (III) Calculate the primary deficit, state what it shows, and comment on the opposition's criticism.
parts.model:
Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit $-$ Interest payments = 14,000 $-$ 7,000 = ₹7,000 crore
The primary deficit shows the borrowing requirement of the government excluding interest payments, that is, the borrowing needed to meet expenditure other than interest on past loans.
The criticism is valid. Half of the borrowing (₹7,000 crore out of ₹14,000 crore) is needed only to pay interest on past loans, and a revenue deficit of ₹6,000 crore means borrowing is also used for current expenditure that creates no assets. Such borrowing adds to future interest burden and may push the government into a debt trap.

points.t: Primary deficit = 14,000 $-$ 7,000 = ₹7,000 crore
Meaning: borrowing requirement excluding interest payments
Comment: half the borrowing pays interest and revenue deficit is financed by borrowing, raising future burden / debt trap

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Answer the following questions for a hypothetical economy (all figures in ₹ crore).

parts.q: (I) The saving function of the economy is $S = -50 + 0.25Y$ and autonomous investment is 100. Calculate (a) the equilibrium level of income, and (b) consumption expenditure at the equilibrium level of income.
parts.model:
(a) At equilibrium, planned saving = planned investment:
$-50 + 0.25Y = 100$
$0.25Y = 150$
$Y$ = ₹600 crore
(b) Saving at equilibrium $= -50 + 0.25 \times 600 = 100$
Consumption $= Y - S = 600 - 100$ = ₹500 crore

points.t: Equilibrium condition: $-50 + 0.25Y = 100$
Equilibrium income = ₹600 crore
Consumption = 600 $-$ 100 = ₹500 crore

parts.q: (II) With the help of a numerical example, explain the working of the investment multiplier, assuming that the marginal propensity to consume is 0.75 and investment rises by ₹100 crore.
parts.model:
Multiplier $k = \frac{1}{1 - MPC} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.75} = 4$, so the final increase in income is $4 \times 100$ = ₹400 crore.
Working: the extra investment of ₹100 crore becomes income of those who produce the capital goods (round 1: income rises by 100). They spend 75% of it, so consumption and the income of others rise by 75 (round 2). Those receiving it spend 75% again, raising income by 56.25 (round 3), and so on. Each round is smaller than the last.
RoundIncrease in incomeIncrease in consumption
110075
27556.25
356.2542.19
.........
Total400300
Total increase in income $= 100 + 75 + 56.25 + \dots = \frac{100}{1 - 0.75}$ = ₹400 crore.

points.t: Multiplier $k = \frac{1}{1-0.75} = 4$
Round-wise working: spending out of each round's income becomes income for others (100, 75, 56.25 ...)
Total increase in income = ₹400 crore

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Which of the following was NOT a part of the trade policy reforms introduced in India in 1991?
(Choose the correct option)
options: Dismantling of quantitative restrictions on imports and exports
Raising import duties to protect domestic industries
Removal of licensing procedures for imports
questions.sol: The trade policy reforms aimed at removing protection: quantitative restrictions were dismantled, tariff rates were reduced and import licensing was removed. Raising import duties for protection was a feature of the earlier inward-looking policy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following statements: Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Choose the correct option from those given below:
Assertion (A): Diversification of rural employment into activities such as animal husbandry, poultry and fisheries is needed in rural India.
Reason (R): Depending only on crop farming for a livelihood carries greater risk.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.sol: Both statements are true, and R explains A: since depending only on farming is risky (output depends on rainfall and the weather), shifting part of the workforce to allied and non-farm activities is needed to reduce risk and provide productive, sustainable livelihoods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Identify which of the following were land reform measures introduced in India after independence.
(i) Abolition of intermediaries
(ii) Ceiling on the size of land holdings
(iii) Use of high yielding variety (HYV) seeds
(iv) Minimum support prices for crops
(Choose the correct option)
questions.sol: Land reforms aimed at equity in landholding: abolition of intermediaries such as zamindars, and land ceilings. HYV seeds belong to the Green Revolution, and minimum support prices are a price policy, not land reform.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following statements carefully:
Statement 1: The Great Leap Forward campaign was launched in China in 1978.
Statement 2: Under the commune system in China, people collectively cultivated land.
In light of the given statements, choose the correct option from the following:
options: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.
questions.sol: Statement 1 is false: the Great Leap Forward was launched in 1958; 1978 is the year of China's economic reforms. Statement 2 is true: under the commune system people cultivated land collectively.
questions.chapter: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Which of the following workers is a part of the formal sector?
(Choose the correct option)
options: A rickshaw puller who owns his rickshaw
A helper in a private shop that employs 5 hired workers
A farmer cultivating his own land
An accountant in a private company that employs 50 hired workers
questions.sol: All public sector establishments and those private sector establishments which employ 10 or more hired workers are formal sector establishments. Only the company with 50 hired workers qualifies.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
A bank in the USA hires a firm in Bengaluru to handle its customer-care calls and keep its accounts. This is an example of ________.
(Choose the correct option to fill up the blank)
questions.sol: Outsourcing is the hiring of regular services from external sources, often from other countries, which were earlier provided internally. It grew rapidly with globalisation and modern communication technology.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Which of the following is NOT a function of the environment?
(Choose the correct option)
options: It supplies renewable and non-renewable resources.
It provides aesthetic services such as scenery.
It creates non-renewable resources as fast as they are used up.
questions.sol: The environment supplies resources, assimilates waste, sustains life and provides aesthetic services. Non-renewable resources get exhausted with use; they are not replenished as fast as they are used.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Which of the following describes India's occupational structure on the eve of independence?
(Choose the correct option)
options: The manufacturing sector had the largest share of the workforce, about 50 per cent.
The agricultural sector had the largest share of the workforce, about 70-75 per cent.
The services sector employed the largest share of the workforce.
The workforce was almost equally divided among agriculture, manufacturing and services.
questions.sol: On the eve of independence, agriculture employed about 70-75 per cent of the workforce, while manufacturing and services accounted for only about 10 per cent and 15-20 per cent respectively.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Identify the correct statements about Pakistan's development experience.
(i) Pakistan follows a mixed economy model with co-existence of public and private sectors.
(ii) Pakistan introduced economic reforms in 1988.
(iii) Growth of agriculture in Pakistan was based mainly on an institutional process of technical change.
(iv) Pakistan announced its first Five Year Plan in 1956.
(Choose the correct option)
questions.sol: Pakistan follows a mixed economy model, began reforms in 1988 and announced its first five year plan (now called the Medium Term Development Plan) in 1956. Its agricultural growth depended on good harvests rather than on technical change, so (iii) is wrong.
questions.chapter: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following statements carefully:
Statement 1: Under demonetisation in November 2016, ₹500 and ₹1,000 currency notes ceased to be legal tender.
Statement 2: The Goods and Services Tax is a direct tax levied on the income of individuals.
In light of the given statements, choose the correct option from the following:
options: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.
questions.sol: Statement 1 is true: in November 2016 the old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes were withdrawn as legal tender. Statement 2 is false: GST is an indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following text carefully:
The government of a country sold 20% of its shares in a profit-making public sector power company to the public and to financial institutions. The government still owns 80% of the shares and continues to manage the company.

parts.q: (I) Identify the policy indicated in the text.
parts.model: Disinvestment: the sale of a part of the government's equity in a public sector enterprise (a form of privatisation).

points.t: Disinvestment (a form of privatisation)

parts.q: (II) Explain any two objectives of this policy.
parts.model:
1. To improve financial discipline: sharing ownership with private shareholders puts pressure on the enterprise to use resources efficiently and earn profits.
2. To facilitate modernisation: private capital and managerial capabilities can be used to improve the performance of public sector enterprises. (The funds raised also help the government meet its expenditure.)

points.t: Improve financial discipline of public sector enterprises
Facilitate modernisation using private capital and managerial skills (or: raise funds for the government)

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Farmers in many parts of rural India sell their produce to traders at low prices soon after the harvest. Explain any three measures taken by the government to improve the marketing of agricultural produce.
questions.model:
1. Regulation of markets: markets were regulated to create orderly and transparent marketing conditions. This protects farmers from malpractices such as faulty weighing and manipulation of accounts, so they get fair prices.
2. Physical infrastructure: roads, railways, warehouses, godowns, cold storages and processing units were provided, so farmers can store produce and sell it later at better prices instead of selling in distress.
3. Policy instruments: assurance of minimum support prices (MSP), maintenance of buffer stocks of wheat and rice by the Food Corporation of India and distribution through the Public Distribution System. MSP protects farmers from a fall in prices. (Cooperative marketing, which gives farmers a better price, is also a valid measure.)

points.t: Regulation of markets for orderly and transparent marketing
Physical infrastructure: roads, warehouses, cold storages, processing units
Policy instruments: MSP / buffer stocks / PDS (or cooperative marketing)

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Answer the following questions on the environment.

parts.q: (I) Explain how the use of compressed natural gas (CNG) in public transport is a strategy for sustainable development. Give an example from India.
parts.model:
CNG is a cleaner fuel than petrol or diesel, so buses and auto-rickshaws running on CNG release much less air pollution. Cleaner air protects health and the environment while transport services continue, so present needs are met without harming future generations.
Example: in Delhi, the use of CNG in the public transport system has significantly lowered air pollution.

points.t: CNG is a cleaner fuel, so vehicles cause less air pollution
Example: Delhi's public transport on CNG lowered air pollution

parts.q: (II) State the meaning of global warming and explain any one of its effects.
parts.model:
Global warming is a gradual increase in the average temperature of the earth's lower atmosphere, caused by the rise in greenhouse gases (such as carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels, and methane) since the Industrial Revolution.
Effect: the polar ice caps and glaciers melt, so the sea level rises. This causes flooding of low-lying coastal areas and can displace the people living there. (Other valid effects: more frequent tropical storms, disruption of drinking water supplies, changes in habitats of plants and animals, spread of tropical diseases.)

points.t: Meaning: gradual rise in the average temperature of the earth's lower atmosphere due to more greenhouse gases
One effect explained, e.g. melting of polar ice raises the sea level and floods coastal areas

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
When the Green Revolution began, there were fears that it would widen the gap between small and big farmers, and that small farmers who grew high yielding variety (HYV) crops could lose everything in a pest attack.
Explain how the steps taken by the government ensured that these fears did not come true.
questions.model:
1. Access to inputs for small farmers: only big farmers could easily afford the inputs (fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation) needed with HYV seeds. The government provided loans to small farmers at low rates of interest and subsidised fertilisers, so that small farmers could also obtain the inputs and benefit from the new technology. This prevented a widening of the gap between small and big farmers.
2. Protection against pests: HYV crops were more prone to pest attacks. The services rendered by research institutes established by the government (such as advice and support to farmers on dealing with pests) considerably reduced the risk of small farmers being ruined by a pest attack.

points.t: Loans at low interest rates to small farmers
Subsidised fertilisers, so small farmers could also afford inputs and the gap did not widen
Research institutes set up by the government
Their services reduced the risk of loss from pest attacks for small farmers

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: State the meaning of worker-population ratio. Explain any two reasons why it is higher in rural areas than in urban areas of India.
questions.model:
Meaning: worker-population ratio is the percentage of the total population that is engaged in work. It is an indicator used to analyse the employment situation in a country.
Reason 1: People in rural areas have limited resources to earn a higher income, and their economic condition does not allow them to stay at home, so more of them take part in the employment market.
Reason 2: Many people in rural areas do not go to schools, colleges and training institutions, or discontinue studies midway to join the workforce. In urban areas, a considerable section is studying in educational institutions, and urban people can wait for jobs that suit their qualifications and skills.

points.t: Meaning: percentage of total population engaged in work
Reason 1: limited resources/poverty means rural people cannot stay out of work
Reason 2: fewer rural people are in education, while urban people study longer and wait for suitable jobs

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Answer the following questions on China's development experience.

parts.q: (I) Explain the main features of the Great Leap Forward campaign launched in China in 1958.
parts.model:
1. Massive industrialisation: the campaign aimed at industrialising the country on a massive scale.
2. Backyard industries: people were encouraged to set up industries in their backyards.
3. Communes: in rural areas, communes were started, under which people collectively cultivated land.

points.t: Aimed at industrialising the country on a massive scale
People encouraged to set up industries in their backyards
Communes started in rural areas with collective cultivation of land

parts.q: (II) China introduced the one-child norm in the late 1970s. Explain any three consequences of this measure.
parts.model:
1. Low population growth: the norm is the major reason for the sharp fall in China's population growth rate.
2. Fall in sex ratio: it led to a decline in the sex ratio, that is, the number of females per 1,000 males.
3. Ageing population: in the coming decades there will be more elderly people in proportion to young people in China, which may create a shortage of workers and a heavier burden of supporting the old.

points.t: Sharp decline in the population growth rate
Decline in the sex ratio
Rising proportion of elderly people relative to the young

questions.chapter: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text:
Read the following text carefully and answer the questions that follow.
Meghpur is a hill village. Five years ago its only school taught up to Class V, and the nearest health centre was 20 km away. Since then, the state government has upgraded the school to Class XII, opened a primary health centre in the village and started a skill centre where young people learn plumbing, electrical repair and computer work.
Lata, who completed a computer course at the centre, moved to Pune, where she works for a software firm and earns three times what she could earn in the village. Her brother Arjun learnt electrical repair and now runs his own shop in the nearby town. The village panchayat has noticed that fewer working days are lost to illness, and that farmers now read crop advice on their phones before sowing.

parts.q: (I) State the meaning of human capital.
parts.model: Human capital is the stock of skill and expertise of a nation (embodied in its people) at a point of time.

points.t: Stock of skill and expertise of the people of a nation at a point of time

parts.q: (II) Identify the source of human capital formation shown by Lata's move to Pune.
parts.model: Migration: people move from one place to another in search of jobs with higher earnings. The higher earnings in the new place outweigh the costs of migration.

points.t: Migration (in search of better-paid jobs)

parts.q: (III) With reference to the text, explain how investment in education and in health contributes to economic growth.
parts.model:
Education: education and skill training raise the productivity and earning capacity of people. Arjun's training lets him run his own repair shop, and Lata earns much more than before. Educated people can also understand and use new technology and information, as the farmers do when they read crop advice before sowing, which raises output. Higher productivity of workers adds to national output and growth.
Health: a healthy worker can work more days and more efficiently. With the health centre, fewer working days are lost to illness in Meghpur, so the village produces more. Healthier people also have a longer working life, which raises the total supply of productive labour in the economy.

points.t: Education raises productivity and earning capacity (e.g. Arjun's shop, Lata's higher earnings)
Education helps people absorb new technology and information, raising output (e.g. farmers using crop advice)
Health: healthy workers lose fewer working days (e.g. fewer days lost to illness in Meghpur)
Health: healthy workers work more efficiently and longer, raising the supply of productive labour and output
